meta.title: The C Form: Five Strings Ring Open
meta.summary: The C form's pentatonic window is the open-position box, five of its six strings ringing open, and the most chord-toned of the five windows in this chapter.

spans.text: Twelve dots, two on every string — that's the shape of every window this chapter fills in, and the C form is where it starts. One reminder before the fret numbers arrive:
means string 5, fret 3 — string first, fret second, in that compact form. This chapter leans on it constantly from here.
The C form sits at barre fret
— open — in a window running frets
. Its twelve dots don't need all five: they live in frets
Five of the six strings have their lower dot sitting right at the nut:
— open strings, ringing for free. Only string 2 breaks the pattern, with its lower dot at

instead of the nut. That's the B string doing what it always does in this pathway — shifting a fret out of line with everything around it. Nowhere else on the neck does a whole pentatonic window sit this close to open strings.

props.caption: The same window chapter 1 lit at two roots and chapter 2 lit at eight chord tones. Twelve dots now — every one of the six strings covered.

spans.text: Only four dots here are new since the triad diagram:

— two of them open strings. Eight of the twelve dots in this window were already chord tones, which makes the C form the most chord-toned window of the five you'll meet this chapter: two thirds of it is
. That makes it the hardest window in the chapter to sound wrong in — and the easiest one in which to forget that the open
ringing under your fretted notes aren't chord tones at all.
Play the five open strings this window uses — 6, 5, 4, 3 and 1 — one at a time against a C chord. Two of them, the open
on string 4, aren't in that chord. You're hearing this window's two non-chord tones before you've fretted a single note. Leave string 2 out — its open note isn't in this scale at all.

The reach in this window sits at its edges. Its three-fret strings are 6, 5 and 1 — the two outside strings and the low A string — while the middle of the shape stays compact. That's the opposite of what's coming next: the A form keeps its stretch in the middle of the hand instead.

Because eight of the twelve dots here are chord tones, this is the easiest window in the chapter to practice the habit the whole chapter is building: run the box freely, but pay attention to when a phrase lands on a
and when it lands on the open
instead. With this many chord tones inside reach, there's rarely a good excuse for a phrase to end anywhere else.
